channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: Anthropic Gives Away 5% of Its Shares, Clone’s Muscle Robot, ElevenLabs Steals Podcaster's Voice
gist: TWiST news episode: Calacanis and Lon Harris contrast Anthropic's 5% (~$100B at ~$2T) public-benefit stock pledge, which they fear becomes a discretionary slush fund, with Musk's plan to give a SpaceX share to every US kid via Invest America/Trump accounts. Clone Robotics' CEO pitches hydraulic artificial-muscle androids at ~1/10th the cost of motor humanoids with enterprise torsos from 2027, and the hosts back Chris Williamson's claim that ElevenLabs cloned his voice.

themes.theme: Anthropic 5% equity pledge vs direct share giveaways

insights.claim: Anthropic announced it will put 5% of its stock into a fund for public-benefit projects (pending stockholder approval), worth roughly $100B at a ~$2T valuation, with board discretion to add 2% more for every 50% of value gained above an undisclosed baseline.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris
insights.so_what: Implies a ~$2T private valuation reference point for Anthropic and a growing, valuation-linked dilution overhang for shareholders.
insights.quote: That first 5% that they're pledging alone is worth around hundred billion dollars.

insights.claim: Calacanis models that if Anthropic's value compounds, the original ~$100B pledge plus valuation-triggered top-ups could grow toward a trillion dollars over ~20 years, making it potentially the largest public endowment ever.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Frames frontier-lab equity as a vehicle for unprecedented philanthropic capital tied to AI valuation growth.
insights.quote: we could be talking about potentially a trillion dollars.

insights.claim: Calacanis distrusts Anthropic's public-benefit fund structure, arguing it risks becoming a discretionary 'slush fund' that favors insiders' causes and creates division, versus directly distributing shares.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Governance skepticism around Anthropic's discretionary capital could become a reputational/political issue for the company.
insights.quote: that to me has got a lot of fingerprints on it that it's going to be a slush fund

insights.claim: Lon Harris argues many people do not fully trust Anthropic's leadership to allocate the fund in ways consistent with what most Americans would prioritize, fueling the 'just give me the shares' reaction.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris
insights.so_what: Trust deficit toward AI-lab leadership is a live public-perception risk.

insights.claim: The hosts speculate (non-zero chance, by their framing) that Anthropic's public-benefit vehicle could drift toward quasi-religious ends, citing discomfort with a New York Times article about the company mixing technology with soul/religious overtones.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis; Lon Harris
insights.so_what: Signals a cultural-political line of attack on Anthropic from prominent tech media voices.
insights.quote: I think that that's a nonzero chance that that's their plan,

themes.theme: Invest America / Trump accounts and equity-for-all

insights.claim: Elon Musk responded to Anthropic's pledge by saying shares should go directly to the public and pledged that next year he will give one SpaceX share to every kid in America, 'the first of many'.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris
insights.so_what: Private-company shares being seeded into kids' accounts broadens retail exposure to SpaceX ahead of any liquidity event.
insights.quote: Next year I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America

insights.claim: Calacanis estimates ~3.6M US births per year and a SpaceX share around $150, implying roughly $500M per annual cohort for Musk's gift, with online estimates of a $10B and eventually ~$100B program.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Sizes the Musk pledge; implies a reference ~$150/share SpaceX price used by the hosts.

insights.claim: Calacanis claims he suggested to Brad Gerstner over poker that the Invest America accounts be branded as Trump accounts to win Trump's backing, which is what happened.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Naming policy vehicles after the president was a deliberate political-economy tactic.

insights.claim: Calacanis argues that the ~40% of Americans without equity ownership feel bad about the economy while equity holders feel great, so directly giving people shares (as Michael Dell's $6B did) is a better fix for AI-driven anxiety than nonprofits or the Giving Pledge.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Broad equity ownership is pitched as the political release valve for AI job displacement; supports retail/brokerage account growth.
insights.quote: People who don't feel great, they don't own equities. They don't own a piece of the prize.

insights.claim: Calacanis claims nonprofits waste much of donations on overhead (he cites 60-70 cents on the dollar going to comp and office space), making direct share grants more efficient than traditional philanthropy.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Reflects a founder-class shift away from foundations toward direct equity distribution.

insights.claim: Calacanis predicts that AI will retire entire job categories, like phone operators and typing pools before, perhaps faster this time, and that society will adapt.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Expect automation of routine white-collar roles; investor framing is displacement is manageable if ownership broadens.
insights.quote: There are going to be entire jobs retired just like phone operators and receptionists are gone.

insights.claim: Lon Harris argues that much anti-AI sentiment stems from people feeling excluded from AI's upside, and giving even small equity stakes would shift public opinion on AI.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris
insights.so_what: Equity distribution could reduce regulatory/political backlash against AI companies.
insights.quote: I think you would see opinions about AI generally shift a lot if people felt like I stand to earn a little money if Grock does better.

insights.claim: Calacanis predicts that Google, Microsoft, Apple and Nvidia will be pressured into contributing shares to kids' accounts, and that a few hundred dollars compounding in an index like QQQ could 10x over ~20 years while teaching financial literacy because funds are locked for 18 years.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Potential wave of corporate share contributions to Trump accounts; tailwind for index-fund inflows and brokerage platforms.
insights.quote: they're all going to be kind of pressured into doing this.

insights.claim: Donors can target share gifts by region or community (e.g., Gwynne Shotwell did something for kids in her region; gifts could go to a borough, church or synagogue), per the hosts.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Localized corporate/philanthropic equity giving may proliferate.

insights.claim: Calacanis says the Invest America / Trump account initiative 'solves socialism' and challenges progressive politicians (Sanders, Warren, AOC, Mamdani) to endorse it, and argues Trump and family should pledge half the increase in their net worth during this term.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Shows bipartisan-pressure framing around equity-for-all policy.
insights.quote: this solves socialism

insights.claim: Calacanis says, based on multiple private conversations, that Musk's SpaceX-share giveaway is not timed to a documentary about him; Musk has long wanted to give money away and liked this plan's simplicity, and he expects it to change the 'villain arc' narrative on Musk.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Musk reputational repositioning via philanthropy could matter for his companies' public standing.

insights.claim: Lon Harris notes that owning even a few shares turns people into cheerleaders, citing buying Meta on a dip and rooting for it despite disliking its products.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris
insights.so_what: Retail ownership drives brand affinity—relevant to companies seeding shareholder bases.

themes.theme: Clone Robotics: hydraulic artificial muscle androids

insights.claim: Clone Robotics is building lifelike humanoid androids actuated by hydraulic artificial muscles (McKibben-style: an elastic tube in a braided sleeve that contracts linearly when pressurized with liquid) instead of the DC motors, gears and tendon drives used by Tesla Optimus, Figure, 1X and Boston Dynamics.
insights.speaker: Den Radhakrishnan (Clone Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: A differentiated actuation stack with a separate supply chain could be a defensible alternative in humanoids.
insights.quote: Basically a rubber tube surrounded by a shoelace at a high level.

insights.claim: Clone claims its muscle-based design can be produced at about a tenth of the cost of motor-actuated humanoids, with no gears in the system and a completely different supply chain, even before scale economies.
insights.speaker: Den Radhakrishnan (Clone Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: If true, a 10x unit-cost advantage would undercut gear/motor-dependent humanoid makers.
insights.quote: it can be done at a tenth of the cost to produce of these motor actuated humanoids.

insights.claim: Clone built what it calls the most human-level robotic hands in the world within its first 18 months on a ~$0.5M budget, and has raised $24M total over five years.
insights.speaker: Den Radhakrishnan (Clone Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Capital-efficient hardware R&D; company is still small relative to Optimus/Figure funding levels.
insights.quote: Yeah, I've raised 24 million to date over the last 5 years at this point.

insights.claim: Radhakrishnan argues motor-actuated humanoids like Optimus will almost certainly have subhuman hand strength if they keep human proportions, and that the wrist is the hardest constraint—1X compromised by making the wrist slightly oversized under a sleeve.
insights.speaker: Den Radhakrishnan (Clone Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Highlights a technical ceiling for motor-based dexterous hands in human form factors.
insights.quote: I'd argue his hands are almost definitely going to be subhuman level in in strength

insights.claim: Clone had to develop its own miniaturized hydraulic valves after no valve manufacturer could meet its specs, which its CEO claims could be a billion-dollar valve business on its own.
insights.speaker: Den Radhakrishnan (Clone Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Component-level IP (valves, compact hydraulic power units) is a potential moat and spin-out value.

insights.claim: Clone plans to deploy its first human-level torsos in stationary enterprise settings (assembly lines, manufacturing) as early as Q1 2027, expects a full android within ~6-12 months, and sees home 'robo butlers' about two to three years out.
insights.speaker: Den Radhakrishnan (Clone Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Gives a dated commercialization timeline to track; enterprise-first go-to-market.
insights.quote: could be as early as you know Q1 2027 we'll deploy our first silos with a torto

insights.claim: Clone's bet is that robot intelligence will largely come 'for free' from open models (e.g., an NVIDIA open-model program) with a 6-12 month half-life, so it focused five years on hardware and will later post-train open-weight checkpoints with RL on its own robot data, mocap, human video and simulation.
insights.speaker: Den Radhakrishnan (Clone Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Hardware differentiation over model differentiation in robotics—models commoditize while capital converts to data and compute.
insights.quote: you can convert capital to data you can convert capital to compute

insights.claim: Clone's CEO says it plans to sell robots rather than rent them, targeting an affordable unit (around $25K is plausible at scale) plus a luxury 'Louis Vuitton-esque' line at ~$1M each, and has no intention of becoming an arms dealer of components or selling early.
insights.speaker: Den Radhakrishnan (Clone Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Signals a vertically integrated, ownership-based business model with tiered pricing.

insights.claim: Calacanis believes humanoid robots are three to four years from delivering real value, and frames the economics as robots at ~$10/hour versus a fully loaded ~$30/hour warehouse worker.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Robot-as-labor unit economics frame; timeline for humanoid ROI in logistics.

insights.claim: Radhakrishnan frames lifelike androids as the final frontier of human-computer interaction—the most natural personal computing platform because humans interact with other humans from birth.
insights.speaker: Den Radhakrishnan (Clone Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Positions humanoids as a consumer computing platform, not just industrial automation.
insights.quote: it's the final it's the final frontier of human computer interaction is the way I think about it.

themes.theme: AI safety debate and voice-cloning IP

insights.claim: Calacanis puts the probability of humanity losing control of AI at roughly one in a billion, rejecting doomer estimates like 10%, and disagrees with Elon Musk on this, arguing 'it's software' even if it becomes recursive.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A prominent VC voice dismissing AI x-risk; reflects investor sentiment against safety-driven regulation.
insights.quote: I think like I don't know, one in a billion that we're not going to be able to control this technology.

insights.claim: Calacanis says All-In was the number one podcast two weeks in a row, and that an AI-safety advocate declined to debate the four hosts, opting for Megyn Kelly instead.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Pro-acceleration media platforms dominate tech discourse.

insights.claim: Podcaster Chris Williamson (Modern Wisdom) alleged ElevenLabs' 'Archer' voice copies his own; his video drew almost 800K views in ~48 hours, and ElevenLabs said a different voice actor supplied it but pulled the voice from the platform.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris
insights.so_what: Voice-likeness IP disputes are a growing legal/reputational risk for voice-AI platforms.
insights.quote: Uh the Archer voice has however been pulled from the platform.

insights.claim: Calacanis believes ElevenLabs is guilty of cloning Williamson's voice, says market confusion strengthens his legal case, and argues ElevenLabs should compensate him (e.g., $100K in shares) and license his real voice.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Expect settlement/licensing pressure and possible litigation costs for synthetic-voice vendors.
insights.quote: It is 100% based on his voice.

insights.claim: Public figures are beginning to trademark their image, likeness and voice (Matthew McConaughey cited), and Calacanis predicts every public figure will need to do so.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Emerging likeness-rights regime creates a licensing market for voice/identity.

insights.claim: ElevenLabs runs an 'Iconic Marketplace' licensing celebrity and estate voices (Michael Caine from Nov 2025, Maya Angelou, John Wayne, Laurence Olivier, Hasbro characters like Optimus Prime), priced per project like celebrity endorsement deals rather than per minute.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris
insights.so_what: Licensed celebrity voice is becoming a monetizable marketplace category.

themes.theme: AI-native media operations and world models

insights.claim: Calacanis says AI design tools let his team produce three or four infographics per Substack post daily, work he estimates would otherwise need roughly five full-time illustrators including ~30-50% capacity slack.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Concrete example of AI displacing creative labor in media production.

insights.claim: World-model startup Odyssey posted a video of a simulated fruit-fly brain flying through worlds generated by its Odyssey 3 model, drawing over 5 million views.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris
insights.so_what: World models are attracting mainstream attention as a frontier AI category.

insights.claim: Nathan Fielder's Elizabeth Holmes documentary scored 98% critics and 98% audience on Rotten Tomatoes, and Calacanis notes Holmes and partner Billy Evans are publicly building a new version of Theranos.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Renewed scrutiny of Silicon Valley 'fake it till you make it' culture; Holmes is attempting a comeback venture.
insights.quote: they have been talking publicly about a new version of Theronos
